item.title: Big Boi Revisits The Two Rejections Before OutKast’s Christmas Breakthrough
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Big Boi looks back on how two early setbacks led OutKast to an unlikely opening on a LaFace Christmas compilation.
item.content:encoded:
Big Boi revisited the two times OutKast got passed over before the Atlanta duo landed a Christmas album slot and turned it into “Player’s Ball.”

The assignment wasn’t an obvious fit for two young rappers trying to get Atlanta heard.

The story came up on Big Boi’s Bloodlines & Basslines, in an episode about the setbacks that put him and his sons on different paths.

In an interview with Bullseye, Big Boi recalled finally getting a shot at a single, only to learn it was for a holiday compilation. “It was like they’re trying to end our career before it even started!” he said.

OutKast was passed over twice, and Big Boi and André 3000 had no intention of making a Christmas record that sounded like anybody else’s.

The first title was “Socks and Drawers.” Big Boi explained that instead of reaching for a Christmas story they didn’t recognize, the pair wrote about spending the day at the Dungeon, where making music was the main thing.

Sleepy Brown told GQ that Organized Noize producer Ray Murray had been working on the beat for Left Eye’s group when Rico Wade heard it. Big Boi remembered being given a choice between the beat that became their single and the one TLC used for “Sleigh Ride.” OutKast took the former.

Sleepy said Wade began sketching the scene in the studio, which gave him the idea for the hook. He told Bullseye that Curtis Mayfield’s falsetto helped him find the sound. LaFace later took out the sleigh bells and changed the holiday reference in the hook, Big Boi recalled, so the single could stay on the radio after Christmas.

The single topped the rap chart and helped carry Southernplayalisticadillacmuzik, OutKast’s 1994 debut, well past that first holiday. RCA dates the release to November 19, 1993, and still lists the Christmas mix.

Decades later, Big Boi started the podcast with his sons Bamboo and Cross, putting the story in a conversation about what people do after hearing no. He had turned down the idea of doing a podcast until he could make it a conversation with his kids.

OutKast entered the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2025.

item.title: Eminem’s Publishers Add 108 Examples To Suno Copyright Lawsuit
item.dc:creator: Grouchy Greg Watkins (@GrouchyGreg)
item.description: Eminem's publishers add 108 alleged AI outputs tied to 26 songs, challenging Suno's claim it blocks artist and song prompts.
item.content:encoded:
Eminem‘s music publishers have added 108 examples to their federal lawsuit against Suno, saying the AI platform generated tracks that used lyrics or musical elements from 26 copyrighted works.

The new filing challenges Suno’s claim that its service does not allow requests for specific artists or songs.

Eight Mile Style and Martin Affiliated filed an amended complaint on November 19 in the Northern District of California. Eminem, whose real name is Marshall Mathers, is not a plaintiff.

The publishers say Suno’s statement after the original filing prompted them to present more examples.

They describe the new material as “108 further examples of additional infringing output of twenty-six of the Works,” and identify recordings that Suno users made publicly available.

The added examples include tracks whose source works the publishers had already named, rather than a new list of songs being added to the lawsuit.

The revised filing lists titles including “Mockingbird,” “Stan,” “Without Me” and “The Real Slim Shady.” The publishers submitted the tracks in a new exhibit and allege that many of the recordings imitate Eminem’s voice.

Eight Mile Style’s initial complaint already identified 269 compositions. It also gave examples involving specific songs, including a generated version of “Lose Yourself” that the publisher alleged repeated the song’s lyrics verbatim.

The 269 works are musical compositions, the underlying music and lyrics, rather than a tally of the individual audio files Suno is accused of generating.

The publishers still seek up to $40.35 million in statutory copyright damages as an alternative to actual damages and profits, along with other relief.

Suno’s response to the initial suit was that it makes original music and prohibits unauthorized uses of artists’ work, the company told CBS Detroit.

In a separate company statement, CEO Mikey Shulman wrote, “Unlike many AI music platforms, we’ve never allowed prompts for specific artists or copyrighted songs.” Shulman wrote that Suno strips artist names from prompts and redirects requests toward musical characteristics.

The publishers first sued Suno on November 6. They also claim the company copied protected compositions to train its music generator and stripped out information used to identify the works.

The publishers have asked a jury to hear the case.

item.title: Mathew Knowles Opens Destiny’s Child’s 2001 BRIT Awards Vault
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Mathew Knowles shares a backstage look at Destiny's Child's 2001 BRIT Awards appearance, from rehearsals to getting dressed.
item.content:encoded:
Mathew Knowles opened his Destiny’s Child archive and put a 30-minute look at the 2001 BRIT Awards on YouTube.

The group’s manager and Beyoncé’s father posted the footage, offering a view of the work that went into the trio’s London appearance.

“In early 2001, London was the test I cared about most,” Knowles wrote in the video’s description. He recalled that a major American act couldn’t count on its success at home carrying over to Britain.

He wanted the group ready for a show that, to him, could tell them where they stood with the industry there.

“People see four minutes on television and assume that’s the job. It isn’t,” Knowles wrote.

He described a day of choreography, wardrobe and rehearsals. Solange was there with Beyoncé, Kelly Rowland and Michelle Williams, years before she would collect a Grammy of her own.

The ceremony took place at Earls Court 2 in London on February 26. Destiny’s Child had just picked up their first Grammy for performing “Say My Name.” The songwriters won Best R&B Song for the same track that night.

Beyoncé and a shocked Eminem greeted each other backstage, with D12 also present.

The British charts had been good to both Destiny’s Child and Eminem by the time they were on the same bill.

The group’s “Independent Women Part I” and his “The Real Slim Shady” had each reached No. 1 in the UK the year before. The Destiny’s Child single came from the Charlie’s Angels soundtrack, and Beyoncé helped write and produce it.

Eminem performed “I’m Back” and “The Real Slim Shady” at the ceremony, and the BRITs named him Best International Male.

Destiny’s Child had another UK No. 1 that spring with “Survivor,” and the album with the same name also topped the British chart.

Knowles has brought out early material from the group before. In 2019, he put out a book and a 15-track album from the Girls Tyme years.

The Houston group performed on Star Search before taking on the name Destiny’s Child.

In 2017, Eminem and Beyoncé released “Walk On Water,” the single that became the opening track on his album Revival.

item.title: Diddy’s Former Chief Of Staff Could Still Face Sex Trafficking Claim
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: A judge delayed a decision until December on the civil sex trafficking claim against Diddy's former chief of staff.
item.content:encoded:
A Los Angeles County judge delayed a decision until December on whether Diddy‘s former chief of staff, Kristina Khorram, must face a civil sex trafficking claim from former assistant Phillip Pines.

At Friday’s Beverly Hills hearing, Pines’ lawyer, Heidi Chang, asked for time to address whether Khorram was shielded from liability while acting as Combs’ agent, Courthouse News reported.

Judge Edward B. Moreton Jr. granted the request over Combs’ lawyers’ objections. His earlier ruling did not decide whether Pines proved the allegations.

Pines alleges Khorram arranged an encounter that Diddy described as a loyalty test.

He says she knew beforehand that Diddy would pressure him into sex with a guest, and that Khorram benefited from her alleged participation through continued employment and related benefits.

Khorram argued that the amended complaint did not adequately allege that she knew about the alleged coercion.

She also disputed whether employment benefits could satisfy the law. Moreton said Pines alleged advance knowledge and that the statute does not exclude employment benefits.

“These facts are sufficient to support a sex trafficking claim,” Moreton wrote.

The proposed decision would reject separate sexual battery, gender violence, harassment, wage and unfair competition claims against Khorram without giving Pines another chance to revise them.

Pines alleged Khorram had the power to fire him and could direct his work at all hours. Moreton wrote that supervising Pines did not establish that Khorram had authority over corporate policy.

That authority was central to whether she could be held liable for wage violations.

Pines worked as a personal assistant for Diddy’s company and says he was tasked with setting up and cleaning up after private parties.

Khorram has denied wrongdoing, and previously challenged the allegations when she asked the court to throw out Pines’ original complaint.

item.title: Snoop Dogg Backs Bigg Jah’s First Movie & Takes A Role In It
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Snoop Dogg joins Bigg Jah on both sides of the camera as the Los Angeles comedian brings his first feature film to Tubi.
item.content:encoded:
Snoop Dogg plays a neighborhood OG in Bigg Jah’s first feature film, but his name is on more than the cast list.

He also executive produced Bigg Homies, a South Los Angeles comedy that starts streaming on Tubi on Tuesday, November 24.

Bigg Jah talked about getting Snoop on board and making the jump to features in an interview with REAL 92.3.

The film puts him in front of the camera as Rodeen, a guy with a reputation in the neighborhood and a problem he can’t talk his way out of. The money meant to save his mother’s house goes missing, so Rodeen has to get it back before she loses the place.

Snoop plays Juan Carlos, an older figure who knows the neighborhood and what goes on in it.

The 97-minute film also features Kontravious Harrell, Hope Flood and Eddie Woods. Bigg Jah directed it and wrote it with Kenn Edwin.

Bigg Jah had been posting stand-up sets online before his sketches caught on.

On the Killin It podcast, he recalled spotting six cents in his YouTube revenue and realizing he could bring over the one-minute clips he’d already made for Instagram.

One of the projects he built for an online audience, The Lesbian Homie, became a series that Tubi picked up for its first slate of exclusive creator shows.

That slate also included his anthology L.A.U.G.H., short for Life Ain’t Usually Great Here, which draws on life in Los Angeles.

Snoop has already worked on both sides of the camera in The Underdoggs, playing a former football star who ends up coaching kids and producing the film through Death Row Pictures.

Snoop and longtime producing partner Constance Schwartz-Morini came up with the original pitch for that movie.

item.title: David Banner Opens Up About Therapy, Burnout And Almost Quitting Hip-Hop
item.dc:creator: Chuck Creekmur (@ChuckCreekmur)
item.description: David Banner tells Chuck “Jigsaw” Creekmur why he nearly quit Hip-Hop, what he sacrificed for his career and how therapy helped him find joy in rap again.
item.content:encoded:
David Banner had just watched his “Where You From?” video light up Times Square when we sat down to talk. I’d never seen him happier. Nearby was a cameraman, an interviewer and one of her best friends to bear witness and document the moment. Occasionally, he’d take pictures with fans, some of which noticed it was Banner on the big screen amid the New York City hustle.

T.I., Juicy J and Duke Deuce appear on the record, but Banner was there alone. In the black truck on the way to WonWorld studio, Banner talks to T.I. sharing the moment. It was hard to believe there was a time when his biggest dream was just getting somebody to hear his music. After about 25 years of friendship, I’d seen plenty of versions of David Banner. This version wanted his friends to see how happy he was. 

Before Times Square, Banner came up in Jackson, Mississippi, getting local radio play and recording as one half of Crooked Lettaz. His 2003 major-label debut, Mississippi: The Album, put “Like a Pimp” alongside “Cadillac on 22’s,” a song that invoked the death of Andre Jones in a Mississippi jail. He went on to produce “La La” for Lil Wayne’s Tha Carter III.

But the life in music is tough. Banner says a chance to tour with Wayne around that album came, but he was too exhausted to leave the house. Banner reveals what therapy helped him admit, and what he gave up to become David Banner. Somehow, being happy has been normalized in a man named after a character that was an iconically tortured soul.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity. There’s nothing like this spirited conversation. Watch/read below.

AllHipHop: We just left Times Square, where you debuted your new video. How did that feel?

David Banner: My therapist has helped me through a period in my life where, a lot of times, man, and I don’t know whether it’s racism, I don’t know whether it’s America, but sometimes we forget the things that we prayed for, we were blessed with. How many people on this planet can honestly say that their childhood dream came into fruition? And we get all depressed and get mad when our dream used to be, “I just want somebody to hear my music.”

I had some of my hardest friends out there with me, bro. But I wanted them to see me have this childhood exuberance, man, ’cause I’m tired of playing like I’m not happy.

This is the first time in my career, and this is actually sad, it’s the first time I ever had fun, really, in Hip-Hop. I’m having a great time, dog. Would you have ever thought, all the time that you’ve known me, that I would have gone from the David Banner who didn’t smile to, I’m sort of like the logo for Black male happiness now?

AllHipHop: I was listening to Mississippi: The Album, and it was super aggressive. It feels more thoughtful now. What do you attribute that to?

David Banner: I don’t think there’s ever been an album that reached the heights that my album did that had the historical references. Not just what we’re going through right now, but what our people went through in the past, especially in the South.

I think on the first album, bro, I was so confused. And now that I’ve had therapy and I’m a little bit older, and I’m comfortable enough in my manhood to say that I was hurt. I was confused. Even my anger, which now is joy, I didn’t understand why certain regions didn’t love us the way that we love them.

I realized Hip-Hop didn’t love me, or don’t love me, the way that I love them. But it’s OK. I wasn’t never going to rap again. I was done. I was going to do like Tim Duncan. When I say I’m done, I’m just gone and you’ll never see me again.

AllHipHop: You said you’re rapping better than ever. What happened when Young Dro sent you his verse?

David Banner: Dro gave me this verse, bro. It was one of the most inspirational verses on this planet. It was jamming. But I called him back, and I knew it was strange for him to hear it coming from David Banner. I was like, “Dog, I need some hoes. I need some colors. I need some flipping paint. I need some Polo.” He was like, “For real, Banner?” I was like, “Yeah.” He said, “Give me an hour.”

And he came back with that verse in an hour. Besides Ab-Soul, I never had nobody that had me go to the dictionary. Dro had me call a preacher, son. I didn’t know what hermeneutics was.

AllHipHop: What is it, bro?

David Banner: You have to look it up. You’re going to have to work for it like I worked for it.

Editors note: Hermeneutics is the theory and methodology of interpretation, especially of texts, language, and human expression. 🙂

AllHipHop: You said kids, but you want the wife, too. Isn’t that the dream?

David Banner: No, that’s always been the highest dream. I’ve always wanted to be a father. It’s funny because sometimes it seems like my rap friends are embarrassed to be married.

AllHipHop: Are they, though?

David Banner: A lot of them are married, but they don’t tell us. Them [dudes] been married. Telling us they pimping. You been married. Stop it.

What was I willing to sacrifice? A wife and kids in order to be David Banner. That’s harsh. And I have to deal with that reality every day. We put Hip-Hop before so many things. And I shouldn’t have done it, but that’s the reality of my life.

I was asked to go on tour with Lil Wayne for Tha Carter III. And when the deal came through, I was so tired that I had a mental and physical breakdown. I stayed in the house for seven months. I couldn’t move. I had worked 10 years straight.

AllHipHop: You said you hate to see Hip-Hop reduced to “chatty comments.” What are you hearing from all these rap podcasts?

David Banner: Just about every rapper has a podcast. This is the least amount of information that has been disseminated amongst our people. And we got more microphones cut on and ain’t nobody talking about shit.

We ain’t learned nothing about African culture. We ain’t learning nothing about Indigenous people. We ain’t learned about nothing that’s going on in politics. And we have all the mics that we control and we choose not to say nothing.

On my podcast, we did a whole bunch of debauchery, but we made sure every day we did something to push Black people forward. Whether it was Black businesses, whether it was about disseminating what’s happening to these kids. Y’all, let’s do something.

David Banner will return…

item.title: Chief Keef Puts His “Don’t Like” Platinum Plaque Up For Auction
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Chief Keef puts his platinum 'Don't Like' plaque, an Alex Moss chain and a racing arcade cabinet up for auction in December.
item.content:encoded:
Chief Keef will put the platinum plaque for “Don’t Like” up for auction, along with a custom diamond chain and an arcade racing game from his personal collection.

The plaque marks the record that took a teenage rapper from Chicago’s South Side into the national conversation. Lil Reese appears on the original; Young Chop produced it, and the track landed on Chief Keef’s 2012 debut album, Finally Rich, under the title “I Don’t Like.”

GEMZ also previewed a one-of-a-kind chain with a cartoon face and ALMIGHTY lettering, designed by jeweler Alex Moss. Another lot is a green Off-White puffer Chief Keef wore in his 2020 “Hood” video, down to the black “20” printed on the chest and the orange mountain patch.

Bidding opens December 1 and runs through December 21, according to a GEMZ Marketplace announcement supplied to AllHipHop.

The record moved well beyond the original video when Kanye West and his G.O.O.D. Music crew remixed it. Their version landed on Cruel Summer the same year, taking the sound of Chicago drill to listeners who hadn’t found it on YouTube.

Then there’s the red Cruis’n Blast cabinet, a full arcade game with a seat and steering wheel rather than a handheld collectible.

The company says Keef is its first artist partner and that some bids will be for in-person experiences with him, not objects.

The auction follows a year in which Keef released Skeletor and finally headlined his own show inside Chicago city limits.

Before his earlier Summer Smash set in suburban Bridgeview, Chief Keef told the Recording Academy how strange it felt to go so long without playing near home.

“I’m ready. I know it’s going to be a big thing. A lot of new people probably think I’m a ghost,” he said in an interview.

At the September homecoming, he performed “Don’t Like” with a live band. The band backed him on “Love Sosa” too, another song from Finally Rich, according to the Chicago Sun-Times’ concert review.

GEMZ says it will announce more auction details before the sale, including details beyond the four pieces shown so far.

item.title: Yella Beezy Co-Defendant Would Have Disputed Murder-For-Hire Claim, Lawyer Says
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Devin Brown's lawyer says Brown would have testified that MO3's killer acted in retaliation, not for money from Yella Beezy.
item.content:encoded:
Yella Beezy‘s jury never heard Devin Brown’s account of why Kewon White killed MO3.

Brown’s lawyer says that if Brown had taken the stand, he would have said White acted in retaliation, not because the Dallas rapper paid him.

Attorney Heath Harris made that claim outside a Dallas courtroom, after Brown pleaded guilty to murder and received a 10-year sentence. Harris said Brown spoke with White around the time of the shooting and knew what motivated him.

“He knows why Kewon did what he did. It was retaliation, not remuneration. That’s what Mr. Brown would have said,” Harris told reporters in footage released by FOX 4 Dallas-Fort Worth.

Harris also said the defense would have argued that White already knew where the apartment was before talking to Brown. He said Brown’s account was that he tried to stop a confrontation there, not direct White to the apartment.

Detective Eric Barnes gave a different account at Yella Beezy’s trial.

FOX 4 reported that Barnes said Brown had tracked MO3 to an apartment. Barnes identified White as the gunman and described Jerry Johnson as the go-between who relayed messages among White, Brown and Yella Beezy.

The prosecution’s case against Yella Beezy was that he hired White to kill MO3.

The jury convicted the rapper of capital murder on November 11, and he was sentenced to life without parole.

Yella Beezy’s lawyers had challenged the state’s money trail, including whether a $40,000 withdrawal could be traced to White.

The withdrawal came nine days after the shooting, and the lead detective acknowledged investigators could not link recovered cash directly to it.

MO3 was killed on Interstate 35E in Dallas on November 11, 2020, six years to the day before Yella Beezy’s verdict.

White was convicted of capital murder in September and is also serving life without parole. Brown was due to stand trial on a capital murder charge, but his agreement reduced that charge to murder.

His lawyer’s account came after the plea, not from sworn testimony by Brown.

Yella Beezy’s lawyer, Toby Shook, said after the verdict that he planned to appeal.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Judge Tosses Nearly $10M Lawsuit Against Megan Thee Stallion
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: A federal judge dismissed a $9,999,000 lawsuit against Megan Thee Stallion, Roc Nation and 1501 as factually baseless.
item.content:encoded:
Megan Thee Stallion is out of a federal lawsuit that sought $9,999,000 from her and several music companies.

A New York judge dismissed the case as frivolous after finding no plausible facts to support the man’s claims.

U.S. District Judge Louis L. Stanton signed the dismissal order in Manhattan.

De’Andre Kendrick brought the case without a lawyer while incarcerated in Indiana. The order lists Megan, Megan Thee Stallion Entertainment Inc., Roc Nation and her former label, 1501 Certified Entertainment, as defendants.

Kendrick claimed Megan promised him money and copies of old photos but failed to deliver. The order says Kendrick described the payment as either $250 or $250,000. He sought nearly $10 million in damages and asked the court to make Megan turn over photos and videos.

The court read the complaint as alleging an Eighth Amendment violation as well as claims under state law.

Stanton wrote that Kendrick “does not provide any plausible factual support for his claims and that they rise to the level of the irrational.”

The judge dismissed the whole case and denied him permission to amend the complaint. The judge said an amended filing would not cure the defects because the complaint gave him no reason to believe Kendrick had facts that could make it credible.

Stanton had let Kendrick proceed without paying the filing fee up front in December 2025.

Federal law requires courts to screen complaints filed under that procedure and dismiss cases they find frivolous.

Megan and 1501 were on the same side of this case.

They had previously been on opposite sides of a multi-year fight over her record deal, which they settled in October 2023. That dispute included whether Something for Thee Hotties counted as an album under her contract.

Megan went on to release music through her own company, Hot Girl Productions. Warner Music Group announced in February 2024 that it would handle distribution and provide global marketing and radio promotion while she retained ownership of her masters and publishing.

item.title: Usher & Chris Brown Fans Wait Hours After Tickets Fail To Load
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Usher and Chris Brown fans waited hours outside the Superdome after some Ticketmaster tickets failed to load on Friday.
item.content:encoded:
Usher and Chris Brown had fans outside the Caesars Superdome in New Orleans waiting for hours to get into their Friday show.

Some ticket holders told WDSU they could not get their tickets to load on Ticketmaster’s app or website.

The New Orleans station had a crew outside the venue on November 20.

Reporters saw fans rush through the doors when staff could scan tickets again, after what WDSU described as a temporary return of service.

FOX 8 later reported that Ticketmaster service had been restored after a nationwide outage. Mike Hoss, a communications coordinator for venue operator ASM Global, confirmed the Superdome disruption to the station.

The Superdome told fans on Instagram that tickets already saved to Apple Wallet were still scanning, WDSU reported.

Ticketmaster Fan Support told people unable to load their tickets to “please visit the box office with your confirmation details for further assistance. They will have a record of your purchase.”

The Superdome’s event listing still shows a Saturday, November 21, performance at 7 P.M., with doors at 6 P.M.

It was the second of two New Orleans dates for the co-headliners, added in April after promoters reported strong demand for Friday’s show.

Both dates used mobile ticket delivery. The New Orleans Regional Transit Authority scheduled bus detours downtown for the concert because of street closures near the stadium.

Ticketmaster’s mobile wallet guide tells fans to move eligible tickets into Apple Wallet or Google Wallet before heading to the venue. Tickets saved that way can be presented at the scanner without pulling up the order again.

The New Orleans stop was one of the dates the tour kept after dropping its second SoFi Stadium show earlier this month. Buyers for that November 16 date received cancellation notices, while the previous night’s Los Angeles performance stayed on the schedule.

Fans in Atlanta also petitioned for refunds or a makeup show after an earlier stop started late and the singers performed separately. That petition covered the opening Atlanta show on November 5 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium.
